articles.title: Derry: Aberfoyle GP surgery halts routine appointments due to 'tsunami' of demand
articles.summary: Aberfoyle Medical Practice in Derry says its doctors are treating 60 patients each every day.
articles.body:
A GP surgery has suspended all routine appointments due to what it calls a "tsunami" of demand.

It is the second time in a week that Aberfoyle Medical Practice in Londonderry has told patients that it is not offering routine appointments - either in person or online.

Dr Donna Mace, who is a partner at the practice and also a member of the Northern Ireland General Practitioners' Committee, said the practice was currently dealing with unprecedented demand.

In real terms, that means their doctors are seeing around 60 patients a day, which she said was not safe.

BBC News NI has contacted the Department of Health (DoH).

"Aberfoyle is one of the biggest practices in Derry and we are really fortunate in that we have 11 doctors, social workers, physios, mental health practitioners and counsellors but unfortunately the last few weeks have just not been manageable at all," Dr Mace told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.

"Every single day the appointments have been filled up, so much so, that every on-call doctor is dealing with 60 patients per day.

"In my on-call, that is dealing with emergency mental health patients, patients in palliative care and very ill children and it was just not manageable," she said.

"I am a partner at the practice and we employ four salaried doctors and there was a risk of losing those doctors If we lost them due to stress or resignation because they couldn't cope, that would mean we would lose 100 appointments so we had to manage the risk.

"They couldn't go on and there was a total crisis."

The doctor said the decision was taken due to concerns about patient safety.

"It was not manageable and it was not safe, no patient is going to appreciate if we miss something because we have less than the usual 10 minutes with them," she said.

The doctor said they could only deal with urgent appointments and apologised to all those affected.

In October, the practice saw more then 4,000 patients face-to-face, handled 1,500 telephone consultations and dealt with nearly 9,000 prescription issues.

The practice would review the situation on a "day-to-day basis" to determine when it could reopen routine appointments.

articles.title: Penn. Teenager Could Become the First Gen Z Saint, 6 Years After Her Death from Brain Cancer at 18
articles.summary: The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops has voted to move Maria Middleton’s process of sainthood forward, but Pope Leo XIV will still need to give his approv...
articles.body:
Pennsylvania teenager Maria Middleton, who died of brain cancer at age 18 in 2020, could become the Catholic Church's first Gen Z saint

The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops voted to advance the cause of beatification and canonization for Middleton at a Nov. 17 meeting, but Pope Leo XIV will need to sign off on the process before she can become a saint

Middleton, who was known for her strong faith and charity work, "lived out the Christian virtues of faith, hope and love and full trust in God's Providence," the USCCB said

A Pennsylvania teenager could become the Catholic Church's first Gen Z saint, six years after her death.

On Tuesday, Nov. 17, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB) voted to advance the cause of beatification and canonization for Maria Middleton, who died of brain cancer at age 18 on Oct. 8, 2020, after Philadelphia Archbishop Nelson J. Pérez filed a petition, per a USCCB release .

The organization said Middleton, who was born in 2002 and grew up in Bucks County, "lived out the Christian virtues of faith, hope and love and full trust in God's Providence."

It added that, as a child, she "prepared meals for the elderly, collected Christmas presents, filled Easter baskets for children, and visited residents at a local nursing home," as well as volunteering extensively with her local church.

Maria's parents, Susan and Brian Middleton, told ABC affiliate WPVI they were still trying to comprehend the development. "Sainthood is attainable. God created us to be saints," Susan said, with Brian adding, "We're sort of living in a space somewhere between heaven and earth."

They paid tribute to their daughter, who loved Taylor Swift , dancing, her pets and telling jokes. "Our favorite Maria quote is, 'You don't have to be weird to be holy,' " Brian said. "She was in every way normal, but she had this extraordinary faith and pursuit of virtue."

Middleton was diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor when she was 16, something her mom described as a "nightmare" for the family. They prayed, with people around the world joining them, and Maria even traveled to Uganda on a mission trip while living with her illness.

After her death, people from around the world came to visit her grave at the National Shrine of Our Lady of Czestochowa in New Britain Township, Penn., and the USCCB said there have been reports of visitors being blessed and healed through her intercession with God.

Her family also discovered several of her writings. "We were curious as to what was the last thing physically she was able to write while holding a pen, and she left us with 'Think hope,' " Susan told WPVI.

The phrase has since given its name to a book about the late teenager, as well as the Think Hope Foundation , set up in her memory.

The process of making Middleton a saint still has some more steps to go, WPVI reported. Notices have been posted at nearby churches asking people to come forward with information about her, and a formal inquiry is being planned.

Pope Leo XIV will also need to sign off on the process before her writings are examined and two miracles are attributed to the teenager, per the outlet.

If Middleton is canonized, she would become the fourth saint born in the U.S. and the first Gen Z saint, WPVI reported.

Last September, U.K.-born Carlo Acutis, who died of leukemia at the age of 15 in 2006, became the Catholic Church's first millennial saint . The teenager, known as "God's influencer," was a web designer who used his technology skills to educate people on Eucharistic miracles.

PEOPLE reached out to the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops and the Think Hope Foundation for comment but did not immediately hear back.

articles.title: 'Ghosts of Muzaffarnagar riots haunting Azam Khan': BJP's Sanjeev Balyan rejects 'political revenge' charge
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP leader and former Union minister Sanjeev Balyan on Tuesday said the \"ghosts of the Muzaffarnagar riots\" continue to haunt Samajwadi Party
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP leader and former Union minister Sanjeev Balyan on Tuesday said the "ghosts of the Muzaffarnagar riots" continue to haunt Samajwadi Party (SP) leader Azam Khan, adding that he cannot escape responsibility for the violence.Speaking to PTI, Balyan was responding to questions about Azam Khan's recent release from jail, the SP veteran's allegations that the BJP-led Uttar Pradesh government was targeting him, and whether his return could influence Muslim voters ahead of the 2027 assembly elections in the state.Also Read | 'His kurta is stained with blood': BJP's Sangeet Som reminds Azam Khan of Muzaffarnagar riots" I enjoy listening to Azam Khan's interviews. He speaks interestingly and often expresses his pain, saying this or that happened to him. But perhaps he does not remember the pain he caused us," the former Muzaffarnagar MP told PTI.Balyan alleged that 6,250 people were named in cases related to the Muzaffarnagar riots on Azam Khan's instructions, with thousands subsequently sent to jail."The ghost of the Muzaffarnagar riots continues to haunt Azam Khan, whether those who died were Hindus or Muslims. Most of those who were jailed were Hindus. Perhaps he has been facing the consequences of those actions for the past 10 years," the BJP leader said."Those who lost their lives in the Muzaffarnagar riots, whether Hindus or Muslims, and the families affected by the violence cannot be forgotten. articles.title: Vietnam restaurant blast kills at least six
articles.summary: At least 10 wounded after blast at restaurant in the Dong Da district in Hanoi as rescue operations under way.
articles.body:
An explosion in a crowded residential part of Vietnam’s capital Hanoi has killed at least six people and injured 10, according to local authorities.

The blast occurred at a restaurant in the Dong Da district at about 8am (01:00 GMT) Tuesday, shattering windows, tearing metal shutters from their frames and heavily damaging surrounding buildings and homes, according to local media reports.

The restaurant was full of people at the time of the explosion, which the Ministry of Public Security believes was related to cooking gas. More people are feared to be trapped under the rubble, which rescuers have spent hours searching through, reported Vietnam’s VnExpress newspaper.

One nearby resident described the blast as “deafening”.

“There was a flash of light, and doors, glass and everything around me were sent flying,” the unnamed resident told the state-affiliated VietNamNet newspaper.

Photos published by VnExpress showed the restaurant, located on the ground floor of an apartment block, almost completely collapsed. Rubble was scattered across the narrow street outside, where several cars and motorbikes were damaged or overturned.

Dozens of firefighters and other rescue officials were dispatched to the scene. They were still digging through rubble more than four hours later, said VnExpress, adding that the city’s mayor was also present.

Authorities have since evacuated people from nearby buildings deemed structurally unsafe, said the report.

articles.title: Why are Russian warships off Libya, and will Ukraine’s attack change that?
articles.summary: Ukraine is stepping up ‘long-range sanctions’ attacks on Russian vessels far beyond the battlefield.
articles.body:
Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli has condemned Ukraine’s deadly attack on a Russian warship in Libya, in what Kyiv claimed was an “exemplary” operation.

Libya’s Foreign Ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the Russia-Ukraine war and that its sovereignty and territorial integrity were non-negotiable, according to a statement posted on Facebook on Monday.

“The continuation of the war between Russia and Ukraine gives neither side the right to conduct military operations on Libyan territory or in its territorial waters,” it said.

Sunday’s drone strike on the Merkury, one of Moscow’s newest warships, resulted in the deaths of at least 10 Libyan and Russian crew members, local authorities said.

The attack sent shockwaves through Europe and the Middle East and raised new fears that the months-long war had already spilled over far from the front line.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Ukraine’s attacks represented a “very dangerous trend”.

On Sunday, Ukrainian drones targeted the Merkury in Libya’s coastal city of Benghazi after the Russian corvette docked to refuel and resupply under a cooperation agreement between Russia and Libya’s eastern rival government based in Benghazi. It is led by Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army (LNA), which is based in Tobruk.

Sources told Al Jazeera that the warship was moored in the civilian area of Benghazi seaport, close to a naval base, when it was hit.

In a Monday post on X, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that the attack had been carried out by Ukraine’s intelligence security service, the SBU, and involved seven Ukrainian drones. The strike also destroyed a Russian Ka-27 combat helicopter. A second Russian ship was also hit. Zelenskyy said the cargo vessel Angara was transporting weapons.

“Despite all the enemy’s efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk,” he wrote.

Ukraine’s security service justified the attacks in a Monday statement, saying that both vessels were “legitimate military targets for Ukraine because they directly supported Russia’s military capabilities”.

Satellite images on Sunday showed that most of the vessel ‌‌‌‌had capsized, with only its bow still visible above water. Smoke from the initial explosion rose from the ship’s superstructure. Along the pier, debris from the strike lay scattered around.

However, officials in Libya told the Associated Press that the Merkury was only heavily damaged.

Unnamed sources also told AP that Ukraine had launched the drones from a military base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya.

Tripoli, in its condemnation of the attack on Monday, did not confirm Ukraine’s alleged presence.

Earlier on Sunday, Prime Minister Osama Hammad of the eastern Libyan government said it had submitted an investigation request to the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council.

What’s happening in Libya and why does Russia have a base there?

Oil-rich Libya is a focal point of the long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

The North African country has been divided since 2011, when a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi. Moscow’s close ally was killed later that year.

The UN recognises the western Libyan government in Tripoli, while the Benghazi-based administration in the east is a close ally of Moscow. Russia has long maintained deep ties with Haftar in a bid to keep eastern Libya as a logistical hub for its widening military operations across Africa, including in Sudan and the Sahel region.

In 2024, following the fall of the Russia-aligned regime of Bashar al-Assad, Moscow shifted attention to Libya as a potential new site for the vast military infrastructure it had built up in Syria over the previous decade during the civil war there.

Moscow managed to maintain relations with the new government in Damascus, although its footprint is much smaller, according to analysis by the Atlantic Council think tank. Some estimates put the number of Russian troops there at 1,000, significantly fewer than around 10,000 in previous years.

How significant is Russia’s presence in Libya?

Russia is believed to have planned and funded projects at multiple Haftar-controlled Libyan military bases in its search for a “plan B” following the fall of the Assad regime in Syria: Al-Jufra, Al-Khadim, Al-Qardabiyah, Brak al-Shati, Maaten al-Sarra and Tamanhint.

An estimated 1,800 Russian troops, including those from Africa Corps, which succeeded the paramilitary Wagner Group, are presently based in Libya.

The United States is meanwhile leading efforts to reunite the two Libyan militaries, partly to counter Russia, analysts say, with Washington focusing on relations with the 35-year-old LNA deputy commander and Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar.

That is likely why Moscow has not yet secured a port in the southern Mediterranean: Libya’s eastern authorities do not want to damage improving ties with the US, Turkiye and European partners by giving Moscow port access, which would be more visible and invite scrutiny, unlike the inland military bases, the Atlantic Council noted.

What does Ukraine’s attack mean for Russia?

It means that Ukraine is achieving results in its push to target Russia thousands of kilometres from the battlefield with what Zelenskyy calls “long-range sanctions”, even as Moscow has focused on overwhelming Kyiv with swarms of killer drones daily.

A particular focus is Russia’s so-called ‘shadow fleet’ , the network of tankers Moscow uses to evade Western oil sanctions.

Around the same time the Merkury was hit, a suspected Ukrainian drone struck the Russia-bound dry cargo ship Sparta II in the eastern Baltic Sea, near Finland. Finnish authorities blamed Kyiv, while Moscow called it “terrorism”.

In July, Kyiv said it hit a Russian missile boat and the Iran-linked cargo ship, Anna, in the Caspian Sea, resulting in a diplomatic fallout between Tehran and Kyiv.

Ukraine’s long-range drones have also hit deep inside Russia, targeting oil terminals and other energy infrastructure.

In June 2025, Ukraine’s secret service smuggled components of 117 attack drones into Russia, then arranged and deployed them to hit multiple military bases in five regions. The covert operation, nicknamed Operation Spider’s Web, caused around $7bn in damage to Russian military equipment.

In the Sahel region of western Africa, Ukraine has been accused of working with armed groups fighting against Malian forces and their allied Africa Corps members, although Kyiv denies that.

articles.title: The ‘eighth front’: Why Israel’s influence war in the US is failing
articles.summary: Despite quadrupling its hasbara budget, Israel is losing American hearts and minds, and its PR may be making it worse.
articles.body:
Israeli efforts to maintain the public goodwill of its principal ally, the United States, appear to be continuing despite a series of setbacks.

According to filings with the US Department of Justice’s Foreign Agent Registration Act on October 28, US influencing company Starboard was contracted by Israeli firm LDRS Group LLC, which declares itself as acting on behalf of the State of Israel to conduct “strategic communications and public relations services in the United States to promote the interests of the State of Israel”.

This builds on previous efforts to influence the US public. The Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft estimates that more than $1bn has been spent in direct funding for programmes to influence US public opinion in favour of Israel since the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. That figure stands independent to the fundraising and political efforts of domestic organisations supporting Israel, such as the highly influential American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

US support for the multiple wars Israel has embarked on since the Hamas-led attack of 2023 has been close to unconditional. In addition to the annual grant, agreed under former President Barack Obama in 2016, the US has provided at least $25.5bn in appropriations and at least $21.7bn in military support, according to Brown University’s Costs of War project. Almost as critical has been the diplomatic support, which has seen the US use its veto t o block United Nations Security Council ceasefire resolutions as well as allowing Palestinian full UN membership.

However, evidence that US public support for Israel is collapsing is growing and has, for lawmakers in both countries, become unavoidable. Numerous polls point to growing hostility to Israel, especially among the young, stretching to include those on the right who hold Israel responsible for gulling President Donald Trump into an unwinnable war with Iran that is forcing their own cost of living, and gas prices, still higher.

President Donald Trump’s announcement that the US would end an Obama-era grant to Israel early, made on the day of the US midterms, was widely seen as an attempt to stave off the worst consequences of waning support for Israel across the political divide. But it did little to halt the rout that followed. The heavy spending by AIPAC and its affiliated organisations, estimated at $84m, in support of explicitly pro-Israel candidates, such as Senator Susan Collins of Maine, was largely considered a waste .

“The shift that has occurred in American public attitudes toward Israel is paradigmatic, generational, and lasting,” pollster Shibley Telhami, the director of the University of Maryland’s Critical Issues Poll, said.

“You cannot unsee what you saw in Gaza, over three years. Israeli public relations campaigns are thus swimming against the tide. When they are visibly connected to Israel, they are even toxic, achieving the opposite results, as we have seen in the midterm elections.”

The pro-Israel campaigns are seeing the biggest impact among Republicans, especially among the Evangelical right. “But even there, there is evidence younger people are less impacted by these active and expensive campaigns,” Telhami said.

Concerns that Israel may be losing the battle for American hearts and minds reach beyond the state’s traditional allies on the right. Speaking with US media in May, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attributed the loss of US public support to unspecified foreign states’ manipulation of social media, ignoring the genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 70,000 people, including about 20,000 children, in the past three years. He characterised this as an “eighth front” in Israel’s ongoing wars with regional powers.

In March, Israel quadrupled the budget for its public diplomacy or “hasbara”, to $730m, much of it earmarked for US social media and American eyeballs. In November, it appeared to go further, bringing more than 250 of what Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs determined to be the next generation of US officials, journalists, influencers and community leaders to tour sites associated with the October 7 attack and cement relations with leading Israeli officials.

“Quadrupling the hasbara spend just means they’re more stupid than I thought they were and I already thought they were pretty stupid,” former Israeli ambassador and consul general in New York Alon Pinkas said. “You change the conversation by changing the policy … So far, they haven’t let any foreign media into Gaza. Can you imagine what happens when they do? No amount of spending on their social media is going to mitigate what international journalists find there.”

Israel and its place in the Middle East had already been losing their relevance to the US before the war on Gaza, he said.

Washington had achieved energy security, the bogeyman of the USSR had been consigned to history, China had emerged as an area of critical interest, and both the public and politicians had grown weary of the kind of forever wars, he said, such as the current US-Israel war on Iran that shows no signs of ending.

“Add to that a resentful and angry president in the White House, and you have some idea of the job [potential incoming prime minister, [Gadi] Eisenkot or whoever, has ahead of them: One that no amount of Hasbara is really going to help.”

How far Israeli efforts to entrench US support among future leaders, or to game the country’s social media platforms, might go in reversing negative perceptions of Israel among the American public remains unclear. The midterm elections saw several of the country’s most vocal critics of Israel elected to Congress.

The prospect of renewed war with Iran, initiated through a partnership of two deeply unpopular leaders in the US and Israel, is unlikely to win hearts and minds.

“There’s no doubt that the three pillars of US support for Israel – the public, congressional, and the executive – are at an all-time low, certainly the lowest in my experience,” former State Department Middle East negotiator Aaron David Miller, now a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment, said.

“It’s not just that we’ve seen the US engage in talks over Israel’s advice with Hamas, Yemen’s Houthi rebels and zeroing out aid [in] US weapons, but we’ve also seen a US president talk of his Israeli counterpart in extraordinary terms, and allowing highly critical phone calls of him discussing him to be leaked. However, this doesn’t mean we’re looking at a permanent rupture. A new Israeli government following different policies will take a good part of the tension out of public perceptions and Congressional angst.”

articles.title: Badger cull ruled out by Plaid Cymru government after speculation
articles.summary: Plaid Cymru ministers rule out mass badger cull as part of new plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis.
articles.body:
Plaid Cymru ministers have ruled out a mass badger cull as part of updated plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB).

It follows months of speculation over the Welsh government's intentions, after an expert group warned "a step change" was needed in efforts to eradicate the disease.

While farming leaders have long called for tougher badger controls, a petition against culling has attracted more than 28,000 signatures on the Senedd website in recent weeks.

The Welsh government said it would take "a new and pragmatic approach to TB eradication that is evidence-based and science-led".

Reform calls for badger cull in fight against bovine TB

Young farmer in tears after TB hits 55 cows

Latest figures show nearly 96% of cattle herds in Wales are now TB free.

But the problem - which can be devastating for affected farms - is concentrated, with higher incidence levels in west Wales and along the border with England.

There were 10,090 cows slaughtered following TB testing in the 12 months to June 2026.

Under the previous Labour-run Welsh government, a target was set for Wales to completely eradicate bovine TB by 2041.

But before May's Senedd election an expert group set up to advise ministers warned that goal would "not be met", and called for urgent action and more funding.

The Bovine TB Eradication Programme Board's latest recommendations were published on Tuesday, alongside the government's response.

On badgers, ministers said they were "not pursuing a mass, non-selective cull".

However further research is proposed of the role played by badgers and deer in spreading the disease via new population surveys and fieldwork.

This would then lead to developing "targeted and proportionate" interventions which could include trapping and testing badgers before vaccinating or euthanising them, "where the evidence supports this".

Localised trapping and culling was trialled in Wales on nine farms between 2017 and 2024, but the cost involved drew criticism after hundreds of thousands of pounds was spent on killing a small number of badgers.

Officials told a briefing for journalists that "selective removal" of badgers was a possibility in future, but "[we] cannot give you a timeline".

Changes to cattle testing were also being proposed by the government, to help spot infection earlier.

They will work with the farming industry to explore "safe ways" of moving cattle out of TB restricted herds, to help businesses continue to operate.

Farms experiencing persistent issues and under so-called enhanced management will be offered more choice in how their situation is handled.

There is talk of a new advisory service for farmers and vets - and moves to provide better, more up-to-date data on the latest disease risk.

Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd MS, said bovine TB remained "one of the most serious animal health challenges facing Wales".

"We will not stand by while farmers face uncertainty and anxiety, nor will we pursue a mass non-selective cull," he added.

"Instead, we will be taking evidence-based and science-led action, incorporating the three pillars of cattle, people and wildlife.

"Farmers and the public will rightly judge us on whether we prevent disease and reduce its impact, even when the decisions are difficult."

Ian Rickman, president of Farmers' Union of Wales, said it was "positive to note that targeted and proportionate action will now be taken on TB in wildlife where evidence supports this approach".

"With the loss of over 92,000 cattle and the percentage of herds under Bovine TB having remained stubbornly consistent for the past ten years, this is now the opportunity to intensify the co-working between industry, the veterinary profession, academics and government in order to deliver these recommendations without delay and further explore the wider proposals set out by the Programme Board," he added.

articles.title: Congress questions Jensen Huang’s return and court clears way for toxic detonation in Iowa: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Congress questions Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO.
articles.body: Congress questions Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO. A federal court allows the detonation at an Army ammunition plant in Iowa to proceed despite local opposition. And recent tech outages are fueling a prepping boom. Here’s what to know today. How Congress reacted to Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia Jensen Huang’s sudden return to Nvidia as CEO — two weeks after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy — was met with enthusiasm from the chip giant’s employees, Wall Street and the president himself. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Speaking at the company’s Santa Clara headquarters yesterday, Huang said he would “be a better CEO the second time around.” Major U.S. stock indexes had their best day since April 2025. President Donald Trump confirmed he personally intervened to ensure Huang’s return as CEO. In a social media post, Trump said the federal government had “no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to national security.” But lawmakers on Capitol Hill were more skeptical, and some were angry. “You gotta be kidding me,” Republican Sen. John Cornyn told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement. In a post on X, Cornyn wrote, “No national security risk? Based on what?” Republican Sen. John Kennedy said, “It’s not my job as a public official to tell a private company who to pick for their CEO. That’s up to the board of directors.” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement that the Trump administration appears to have known about Chinese espionage efforts targeting Huang for the past year and that his reinstatement “without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer accused Trump of “putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security.” Two upcoming congressional interviews with Huang are still on the calendar. On Dec. 1, three House committees — the Select Committee on China, the Intelligence Committee and Foreign Affairs Committee — will conduct a closed-door interview with Huang. Two days later, Huang is scheduled to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee. What others in Congress said. articles.summary: Steelers receiver DK Metcalf deflected blame after his ejection for an eye poke of Cooper DeJean, saying, "I was just telling him, stop pushing me."

One day after his ejection for poking at the face of Eagles cornerback Cooper DeJean, Metcalf met with reporters and said what a lot of us have the morning after a rough weekend. "I can't remember." In the third quarter of Sunday's game, Metcalf was disqualified after appearing to poke DeJean in the eye. It was his second personal foul of the afternoon — the first coming when he shoved DeJean after the whistle. He also swiped at an official's hand. Then, when asked if he tried to poke DeJean in the eye, Metcalf said: "I mean, I didn’t try to poke him in the eye. I was just telling him." "Telling him what?" "I was just telling him, stop pushing me," Metcalf said. "That's all I said." If this were a one-off for the eighth-year receiver, he might get the benefit of the doubt. But physical altercations and a lack of contrition have become Metcalf's signature cocktail. BRADLEY CHUBB'S DETAILED VERSION OF ALARIC JACKSON PUNCH INCIDENT PAINTS RAMS LINEMAN AS A HOTHEAD Last December, Metcalf earned a two-game suspension for grabbing a Lions fan by the shirt and taking a swing at him during a game in Detroit. The fan, Ryan Kennedy, said he had been heckling Metcalf by calling him by his full name — DeKaylin Zecharius Metcalf. But a decidedly different narrative emerged when former NFL receiver Chad Johnson said Metcalf told him Kennedy had called him the N-word and called his mother the C-word. Kennedy vehemently denied the allegations. And in a letter to Kennedy three days after the incident, the Lions acknowledged that Metcalf had alleged racist and misogynistic harassment during the NFL's disciplinary process. The next sentence in that letter? "At this time we have not found any evidence that confirms these specific violations." Kennedy, who said his family received threats in the aftermath of the allegations, filed a $100 million lawsuit in February. It's impossible to know precisely what was said in that exchange. What's considerably easier to establish, though, is that Metcalf has yet to publicly acknowledge that what he did was wrong. "It's just a board to me. I'm not going to change the way I play." Later in that news conference, Metcalf was asked if he'd made progress in channeling his emotions so as not to hurt the team. I wrote a column that day for The Seattle Times under the headline "Seahawks WR DK Metcalf has a penalty problem that he won’t admit to." articles.title: Kelsey Hunter: Police fear missing 20-year-old 'may have come to harm'
articles.summary: Kelsey Hunter was last seen in Castle Douglas on Saturday but police activity is focused around a field in a nearby village.
articles.body:
Police searching for a missing 20-year-old woman in Dumfries and Galloway say that it is possible she "may have come to harm".

Dogs, a helicopter and specialist officers have been involved in the hunt for Kelsey Hunter, who was last seen in Castle Douglas at about 17:00 on Saturday.

There has been a large police presence around a field near her home in the village of Springholm and a police tent has been erected.

Police said a 21-year-old man had been arrested and charged in connection with an assault and was due to appear at Dumfries Sheriff Court.

Detectives from Police Scotland's major investigations team and local officers have also joined the search for Ms Hunter.

They said everything possible was being done to find the missing woman.

Det Ch Insp Stephen McGrath said: "Kelsey's family are understandably extremely worried about her and they are being supported by specialist officers at this difficult time.

"We have a dedicated team of officers who are working around the clock to find her and get answers for them.

"While we are keeping an open mind, and continue to hope Kelsey will be found safe and well, we have to consider the possibility that she may have to come to harm."

Police activity is currently focused around the opening to a field near her house in Reoch Park.

An extended police cordon is in place covering a large area of the field, a yellow police tent has been erected and officers remain outside her home.

Officers in white forensic suits have been seen at the entrance to the field and looking around a bridge that straddles a burn running through the field.

Det Ch Insp McGrath said they were trying to build up a picture of her life in the days and weeks prior to her being reported missing and appealed for any friends with information to contact them.

"It is absolutely vital that we find Kelsey as soon as possible and I would again ask anyone with information – no matter how small or insignificant it may seem – to contact us," he said.

Police will remain in the area over the coming days.

Local area commander Emma Dodds said: "Our priority remains tracing Kelsey and getting answers for her family about her whereabouts.

"We have a dedicated team, including specialist officers and national resources, following all lines of inquiry."

She added: "I understand this will be concerning for the local community, but please be assured we are doing all we can to find Kelsey.

"We will remain in the area while our investigation continues.

"Anyone with any concerns, or information, can approach these officers – we are here to help."

Kelsey is described as 5ft4in tall, of slight build with dyed blonde/pink hair. When she was last seen she was wearing a brown jacket and brown boots and was carrying a chequered bag.

Officers have been carrying out door-to-door inquiries and requesting doorbell camera footage from neighbours.

They have appealed for anyone with information about her whereabouts to contact them on 101.

articles.title: One every four minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed since start of Ukraine war, new data suggests
articles.summary: Almost three-quarters of a million Russian soldiers have been killed since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, equating to roughly one death every four minutes, analysis based on leaked official data has revealed.
articles.body: Almost three-quarters of a million Russian soldiers have been killed since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, equating to roughly one death every four minutes, analysis based on leaked official data has revealed. Russian opposition outlets Mediazona and Meduza reported on Monday that by the end of September, 490,000 Russian troops had been confirmed dead by Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat. But accounting for time lags in reporting and including troops who have been reported as missing in action – and are most likely dead – Russian fatalities jump to more than 720,000 since the start of the war, according to the two outlets. That is a staggering number that surpasses Russia’s death toll from the Soviet war in Afghanistan in the 1980s and both Chechen wars in the 1990s and early 2000s – and which the Kremlin has long tried to keep secret. Rosstat stopped publishing demographic data in 2025 to disguise the rising death toll from the war. Mediazona and Meduza, as well as other outlets, obtained the official data after two pro-Ukrainian hacker groups, Cyber ​​Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow, managed to breach Rosstat’s servers earlier this month. CNN cannot independently verify the figures, but the leaked data on confirmed deaths alone corroborates earlier estimates by analysts and Western intelligence – which now appear to fall far short of the likely real death toll. Mediazona and Meduza have long been keeping a tally of Russian losses, based mostly on inheritance documents, death notices and other publicly available documents. But the leaked Rosstat data allowed the media outlets to go a step further, using the same methods and calculations normally employed by actuaries estimating risks and insurance premiums. By analyzing discrepancies between reported death dates and death registration dates, and by comparing these to search notices published by relatives, the reporters were able to extrapolate the number of deaths that have occurred but have not yet been reported to be somewhere around 230,000. Mediazona has kept a tally of troops identified as missing by their relatives from 2023. That database contains 160,000 individuals and almost all of them are likely dead. Mediazona said that based on its reporting, the rate of survival among those reported missing only around 10%. The data shared by Silent Crow showed that the war was the fourth most common cause of death in Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion, after heart diseases; Covid; and stroke and other vascular conditions. It also confirms what has long been suspected – that the losses are not spread evenly across Russia, with poorer areas and ethnic minorities suffering significantly higher casualty rates. In addition, an analysis by the NEST Centre, a think tank that also obtained the data, revealed the scale of Russia’s recruitment of foreign fighters. It identified 6,947 records of foreign nationals killed in Ukraine – the majority of them from the central Asian countries of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkmenistan. Maria Pevchikh, the head of investigations at Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation, said the release of the data shows why Russian President Vladimir Putin is unlikely to seek compromise to end the war. “Putin has no way to ‘step back from public life’ or ‘focus on housing and utilities problems’ after killing 700,000 of his own citizens, and he never will. You don’t retire after something like that,” she said on X. Meanwhile, Alexander Baunov, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, noted the war in Ukraine was Russia’s deadliest conflict since World War II. “We talk a lot about the risk of nuclear escalation. But in terms of human losses, we may already be approaching the scale of a limited nuclear war,” he said. Aby Shukiurov, a demographer and an associate fellow at the NEST Centre, said the Russian authorities “made concerted efforts to conceal the demographic reality of the war.” Shukiurov pointed out that the high death toll has pushed down male life expectancy in Russia to 65.3 years in 2025. That is 3.1 years lower than in 2019 and almost at the level recorded in 2021, the worst year of the pandemic. Meanwhile, female life expectancy continued to rise during the war, reaching a record high of 79.3 years in 2025, he said. Like Russia, Ukraine doesn’t release official casualty data, although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has publicly acknowledged the scale of losses in combat. The most recent research by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in July that the country has endured between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties, including 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities. Baunov said that the combined death between Russia and Ukraine could exceed 1 million. “One million dead is an important psychological threshold. But if almost nobody in Russia knows that this threshold may have been crossed, it is as if it hasn’t been crossed at all,” he said on X.

articles.title: UK sanctions Yemen’s Houthi group and four of its top officials
articles.summary: Group must be held accountable for ‘targeting our partners and innocent civilians’, says Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis as well as four of the armed group’s senior officials.

Announcing the measures on Wednesday, the British government accused the Iran-backed group of “deliberately attempting to undermine stability in the Middle East”.

It accused the four sanctioned individuals – Houthi Interior Minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi, security and intelligence chief Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani, judge Mohammed Moufleh and prosecutor Sarim al-Din Muffadal – of involvement in human rights abuses.

Muffadal, according to the UK government, “is reasonably suspected of having directly perpetrated, or knowingly permitted or acquiesced in, sexual violence, including rape, torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of women detainees”.

Al-Houthi, meanwhile, allegedly oversaw the custody of detainees who were “subjected to torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment”. Such abuses included “electric shocks, beatings and sexual violence”, the UK government said.

The sanctioned individuals are subject to an asset freeze and travel ban, it added.

The UK government said the measures reaffirmed Britain’s view that “Houthi aggression is unacceptable and that the group must be held to account”.

It cited the group’s attacks on vessels in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, strikes targeting civil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and “aggression” in Yemen.

Since seizing Yemen’s capital Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – have controlled much of northern and western Yemen, and Yemen’s internationally recognised government has controlled much of the south. While a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely halted the fighting in 2022, the conflict flared again in July when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.

The group then carried out a lightning offensive in September, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline near Bab al-Mandeb. Government forces launched a counteroffensive last month to recapture territory from the Houthis, but earlier this month forces allied to the government said they would withdraw from areas around the strait and focus on defending Aden.

During the latest flare-up in fighting, Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been targeted in near-daily Houthi rocket and drone strikes. One attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh in October killed 13 people .

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the sanctions sent a message that Britain “will always act in support of British values and interests.”

“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable and they must be held to account,” said Miliband.

articles.title: Iran files lawsuits in US, EU courts: Will it get justice for ‘war crimes’?
articles.summary: As Iran seeks accountability and compensation for alleged war crimes, experts say legal proceedings face steep hurdles.
articles.body:
Iran has filed lawsuits in the United States and European countries for alleged war crimes committed during the US-Israel war, including the missile attack on a school that killed at least 178 people, most of them schoolgirls.

Vice President for Legal Affairs Majid Ansari said on Sunday that Iran has begun legal proceedings in courts in the US and four European countries over “war crimes”, months after the deadly attack on a primary school in Minab in February on the first day of the ongoing war .

The lawsuits will cover the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei , Iran’s official news agency IRNA reported. They will also address the deaths of scientists, military commanders and civilians, as well as attacks on civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, ambulances and emergency facilities.

Speaking at a ceremony honouring the families of children killed in US and Israeli attacks, Ansari said his office is working with the country’s justice and foreign ministries to pursue claims under international law.

The courts in the US and European countries have not been identified, but Ansari said proceedings had been initiated in courts that accepted jurisdiction over the cases. He gave no further specific details.

Experts say the cases in Europe may offer a more viable legal avenue, while proceedings in the US face significant jurisdictional hurdles. But whether Iran can turn these proceedings into meaningful accountability is questionable.

“Iran is pursuing the legal avenues available to it, seeking accountability and preserving evidence,” Saeed Bagheri, an assistant professor in international law at the University of Reading in the UK, told Al Jazeera.

“Compensation may be an objective, but it is far from assured.”

Iran is pursuing its cases in the US and Europe because it has limited access to international courts.

Ansari said Iran was considering filing a case with the International Criminal Court (ICC), which tries individuals charged with the most grave crimes. But Tehran – alongside the US and Israel – is not a signatory to the Rome Statute under which the court was formed in 2002. Iran would, therefore, need an independent basis for jurisdiction, such as a UN Security Council referral.

At the International Court of Justice (ICJ) – the world’s top court that handles legal disputes between states – jurisdiction depends on state consent under Article 36 of the ICJ, said Bagheri.

“Iran cannot simply demand a hearing in either court,” said the expert, who is also a fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law based in Germany.

Amid the legal hurdles, Iran has filed a number of cases in both domestic and international courts accusing the US and Israel of committing war crimes in the June 2025 war as well as the ongoing war. Iran says more than 3,500 people have been killed and 26,500 wounded in the war, along with widespread damage to civilian infrastructure, including schools, hospitals, bridges and energy facilities.

In March, Iran filed a complaint at the Iran-US Claims Tribunal in The Hague, accusing Washington of military aggression, illegal economic sanctions and threats of force. The Tribunal was formed following the 1981 Algiers Accords brokered by Algeria.

On Sunday, Ansari said preparations were under way for a second complaint to the Tribunal over the current war.

In September, Iran’s judiciary issued indictments against 159 senior US and Israeli political and military officials over the assassination of Khamenei and military commanders, judiciary spokesman Ali Kazemi said.

The Iranian judiciary has also said that about 400 cases have been filed with Iranian courts as part of domestic and international legal proceedings, including one involving 350,000 plaintiffs, Press TV reported.

A judiciary official on Monday said that local courts have demanded $290bn in damages from the United States.

A separate civil lawsuit was filed in the US in September by the National Iranian American Council Action (NIAC), a US civil society organisation, alongside several Iranian plaintiffs, including the father of a girl killed in the Minab school bombing. The case seeks a ruling that the US military campaign in Iran was unconstitutional. This case was not brought by the Iranian government.

The Minab school bombing is a large component of Iran’s pursuit of justice in the US and European courts.

In September, a report by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission found that the United States likely committed “war crimes” when it struck the school.

But Iran’s arsenal of evidence to prove that the Minab school bombing was a war crime would have to be wide in scope – civilian deaths do not, on their own, establish a war crime, said Bagheri in Reading.

Iran would need to establish who carried out the attack, what was targeted and what the relevant decision-makers knew at the time, he explained.

Calling a strike accidental also does not settle whether it was lawful or not, said Bagheri.

Investigators must assess whether the military followed the rules of distinction, proportionality and precautions to protect civilians, he added.

“For Minab, the crucial evidence would include targeting files, intelligence assessments, no-strike lists, collateral-damage estimates and records showing when the information was last verified,” Bagheri explained.

According to the UN Mission’s report, the civilian nature of the school was apparent and the US failed in its obligation “to do everything feasible” to verify that it was a military objective.

The report’s authors said that photographs and videos depicting the school before and after the attack showed “readily identifiable features” that it was associated with an educational facility for young children.

“According to public reporting, satellite imagery of the school before the strike also appears to show human figures, readily identifiable as children, gathered in its courtyard,” the report said.

Ultimately, the biggest challenge, said Bagheri, would be linking the evidence of what happened to the decisions, knowledge and intentions of specific military commanders or officials, rather than simply establishing that civilians were killed.

In June, US President Donald Trump said that “nobody” purposefully attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident, for which the Pentagon has not yet published any findings.

The Pentagon launched an internal investigation, but it has not yet publicly released its report.

Both the US and Israeli states, as well as individual officials and military commanders, could potentially be held responsible for the alleged violations, but under different legal frameworks.

State responsibility depends on whether an action can be attributed to a state and whether it breached international law, said Bagheri.

Individual criminal responsibility, meanwhile, can extend to those who carried out, ordered or assisted crimes, as well as commanders who failed to prevent or respond to crimes by forces under their effective control, the expert said.

Rank alone does not matter and investigators must establish what individuals knew, what authority they exercised and what they could have done, said Bagheri.

Still, immunity may also shield some officials from prosecution in foreign courts, particularly serving heads of state, government leaders and foreign ministers.

“Functional immunity for other officials accused of international crimes is more contested and depends on the forum,” said the expert from the University of Reading.

“But I would treat Khamenei’s killing separately. Article 110 of Iran’s Constitution gives the supreme leader command authority, but that title alone does not settle whether he was lawfully targetable.”

His actual military role and the circumstances of the attack matter, he added.

Iran may have a more viable path to pursuing its cases in Europe than in the US.

In some European countries, prosecutors can pursue serious international crimes under universal jurisdiction, regardless of the nationality of the accused or where the alleged offences happened.

But, Bagheri stressed, this route could lead to the prosecution of individuals – not a criminal trial of the US or Israeli governments.

The majority of European Union member states practice universal jurisdiction, according to the European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation (Eurojust). The principle of universal jurisdiction allows the prosecution of individuals suspected of international crimes regardless of where they are committed.

In recent years, EU member states have been successful in bringing a number of perpetrators of international crimes to court on the basis of universal or extraterritorial jurisdiction, with convictions obtained in situations as diverse as Syria, Afghanistan, Rwanda and Liberia, including for crimes dating back 40 years, reports Eurojust.

Still, EU countries have varying requirements to proceed with a case, spanning their own presence, residence, nationality or territorial requirements, said Bagheri.

In his view, victims or civil parties are more likely to find success in producing investigations and preserving evidence than bringing senior US or Israeli officials to trial.

In the US, however, Iran faces “serious obstacles” in pursuing its cases, Bagheri said.

“That does not make them pointless, but getting a complaint before a court is a long way from securing a trial or compensation,” he said.

The first obstacle is sovereign immunity – the country’s Federal Tort Claims Act excludes claims arising in a foreign country and claims arising from combatant activities during wartime, said Bagheri.

Suing individual officials may not get around those protections either, he added.

The US War Crimes Act allows prosecution for certain offences, but neither Iran nor victims can initiate federal criminal cases themselves – that decision rests with US prosecutors, said Bagheri.

Experts point out that securing compensation could prove even more difficult than obtaining an investigation or court judgement.

State property may be immune from seizure, while a company’s links to a defendant do not automatically make its assets available to satisfy a judgement. US sanctions on Iran could further complicate payments, Bagheri said.

An arrest warrant, Bagheri said, does not guarantee that a suspect will be detained. Suspects generally must enter a country willing and legally able to act, he said, adding that an Interpol Red Notice is not an international arrest warrant and does not compel an arrest.

Despite these obstacles, Bagheri said Iran’s proceedings could still serve the purpose: preserving evidence and, where courts reach the merits, establishing legal responsibility.

articles.title: Heat deaths reach record high in UK in 2026
articles.summary: The UK Health Security Agency estimates that the total number of deaths has reached 5,258 for the summer of 2026.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom registered more than 5,000 deaths linked to this summer’s heat, the highest number of such cases since records began in 2016, according to the UK Health Security Agency’s (UKHSA) estimates.

“Summer 2026 was an exceptional summer with the highest mortality observed since 2016 when the UKHSA began publishing annual heat mortality reports,” the agency said on Tuesday in a provisional report, after the UK experienced its hottest summer on record this year.

The UKHSA said the highest number of heat-associated deaths was recorded between June 21 and 28, when an estimated 2,401 deaths were associated with the period of extreme heat.

It comes after Europe experienced another summer marked by prolonged periods of extreme heat , which scientists say are becoming ⁠more frequent and intense because of climate change .

Other European countries have also reported record excess mortality from the heatwaves over the summer.

Researchers from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine estimated that more than 50,000 heat-related deaths occurred in urban areas across 30 European countries during the summer, the ⁠highest toll recorded since 2000.

The announcement of the latest data from the UK comes days after United Nations climate talks ended in collapse on Sunday, as the European Union and others rejected a final deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkiye and Australia.

The EU claimed the draft text was too weak to advance the fight against global warming with no reference to fossil fuels.

The failed talks reflect the struggle by governments across the world to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change, including heatwaves, wildfires, floods and powerful storms – as wars and economic pressures compete for their attention.

articles.title: Will a coastal storm keep balloons grounded for Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade?
articles.summary: Winds will be ramping up throughout Thursday, which could spell trouble for the balloons in the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.
articles.body: Winds will be ramping up throughout the day Thursday and that could spell trouble for the balloons in the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. A low pressure system will track up the East Coast Thursday, strengthening as it approaches the tri-state. Winds will steadily increase in the city as the morning progresses. The big question is, will it get too windy to fly the balloons? It’s going to be a close call. Balloons are grounded when sustained winds reach 24 mph or wind gusts reach 35 mph. When the parade begins at 8:30 a.m., both sustained winds and wind gusts should be below these thresholds. However, by 10-11 a.m., wind gusts could be 35 mph or higher, which would force handlers to ground the balloons. These winds don’t factor in the “wind tunnel” effect that can often increase gusts in the city as wind funnels between Manhattan’s skyscrapers. How quickly the wind speeds increase Thursday morning will depend on how quickly the low pressure system tracks up the east coast. The faster it moves, the quicker it makes it to the Northeast and we feel wind gusts over 30 mph and, eventually, over 40 mph. Peak wind gusts are expected to be between 40 and 50 mph Thursday afternoon and evening. The low pressure system will also deliver rain to the tri-state. The rain will be more of an afternoon and evening occurrence, but there may be pockets of light rain that do dampen the parade.

articles.title: Key Chinese Communist Party figure placed under corruption probe as Xi’s purge escalates
articles.summary: The Communist Party chief of Shanghai, considered one of the potential heirs to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, has suddenly been placed under investigation –– marking an escalation of an anti-corruption purge that’s already ensnared a large swath of the country’s top talent.
articles.body: The Communist Party chief of Shanghai, considered one of the potential heirs to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, has suddenly been placed under investigation –– marking an escalation of an anti-corruption purge that’s already ensnared a large swath of the country’s top talent. Chen Jining, 62, who has run China’s largest city and financial center since October 2022, is facing a corruption charge and is suspected of “serious violations of discipline,” state media Xinhua said on Tuesday evening. It is a stunning downfall for Chen, who was seen as a rising political star and even being mentioned among potential successors to longtime leader Xi by China watchers. Xi, who is all but certain to assume a precedent-breaking fourth term in office next year, has executed an unrelenting anti-corruption drive for well over a decade that has brought down senior political, military and judiciary figures once thought untouchable. The speed and scale that effort has reached unseen levels in recent months. Chen becomes the fourth of the 24 member politburo –– the top-echelon of power in China –– to fall since the last party congress in 2022. The investigation is being conducted by China’s main anti-corruption body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Chen’s last public appearance appears to be Thursday, November 19, when he inspected the headquarters of a Chinese shipping conglomerate. Unsurprisingly, government platforms in Shanghai have quickly taken down posts mentioning Chen. Rising star Trained as an environmental scientist, the urbane and English-speaking Chen rose through the party ranks in the past two decades. Before moving to Shanghai, he was mayor of Beijing and orchestrated the 2022 Winter Olympics Games in the capital. His appointment to the top party job in Shanghai marked a quick elevation. The post usually paves the way for further promotion to the Politburo Standing Committee - the pinnacle of the party’s power structure. Both Xi and China’s former leader Jiang Zemin have followed this path. Prior to his Beijing mayorship, Chen spent over a decade at the Ministry of Environment and Ecology. He also served as the president of the Tsinghua University in Beijing, one of China’s most prestigious academic institutions. After earning a master’s degree in civil and environmental engineering from Tsinghua in 1980s, Chen went to study at London’s Imperial College, where he earned a doctorate degree. Intensifying purge Just in the past two month, Xi’s clampdown of top officials saw the downfall of Beijing’s deputy mayor and a retired former mayor of Chongqing who had withstood several prior political storms. The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission, is now down to only two members with one of those being Xi himself. Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago millions of rank-and-file officials have also been caught in his dragnet. Between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials were convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption, according to official data from the party’s Central Commission of Discipline Inspection (CCDI) – with more than 410 officials purged in the last three years alone.

articles.title: 'Crime over decades': Judge unseals heavily redacted records on Ilhan Omar's home search. Did her father misrepresent her birth year so that she could become US citizen as a minor?
articles.summary: A federal investigation into Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar has been examining alleged crimes dating back to 1980, according to newly unsealed court
articles.body: A federal investigation into Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar has been examining alleged crimes dating back to 1980, according to newly unsealed court documents that shed light on the search of her Washington, DC, home last month. The heavily redacted records, released Monday by a federal judge, indicate that investigators are pursuing a pre-indictment case involving Omar and possible immigration fraud. However, the documents do not specify the alleged offences or disclose whether prosecutors are preparing particular criminal charges against her.One of the government filings stated: "The United States believes ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress." The filing also said that the investigation has nothing to do with her professional life.The records were made public following a lawsuit by more than a dozen news organisations seeking access to documents related to the federal search of Omar's residence. The 169-page collection contains extensive redactions, and a 67-page affidavit supporting the search warrant remains sealed.\Why did federal agents search Ilhan Omar's home?Federal authorities applied for a search warrant on October 2, seeking permission to search Omar's Washington, DC, residence for documents and other evidence relating to alleged violations involving the Congresswoman. A judge approved the warrant on October 9, and Homeland Security Investigations agents executed it on October 12.The warrant authorized agents to seize papers, records, photographs, documents, physical objects, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers and cellphones registered to or used by Omar. Omar said that agents took 17 items from her home, including several cellphones, notebooks, computers and her passport. The seized items reportedly also included a children's book and a vintage camera belonging to her husband, political consultant Tim Mynett.The search warrant referred to Omar by the names "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar" and sought evidence of alleged violations dating from 1980 to the present. Three days before the raid, a judge had ordered the warrant sealed, citing concerns that public disclosure could lead to flight from prosecution, destruction or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses and serious jeopardy to the investigation.What is the immigration fraud investigation about?Federal authorities are examining possible immigration fraud involving Omar or members of her family who fled war-torn Somalia in the 1990s. They are probing whether Omar's birthday was listed as October 4, 1982, rather than a year earlier, so that she became eligible for US citizenship as a minor when her father naturalized in 2000. Another focus is her 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, a British national whom investigators reportedly suspect could be her brother. The two remained legally married until 2017.Omar has repeatedly denied knowingly marrying her brother. Asked about the allegation during an October 21 interview on MS NOW's 'All In with Chris Hayes', she said: "Not to my knowledge."Investigators have revisited records relating to the marriage because Omar reportedly filed joint tax returns with her first husband, Ahmed Hirsi, at least twice during the period she was legally married to Elmi. Elmi has described himself as gay and is a PhD researcher at the University of Bristol, where his work includes research on queer violence in Kenya.The investigation is also reportedly examining the immigration paperwork of some of Omar's relatives. The Wall Street Journal previously reported that authorities had issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to family members, seeking testimony before a Minnesota grand jury.Omar, 44, immigrated to the US from Somalia in 1995 and became a naturalized citizen in 2000. articles.title: Israeli air strike kills senior Hamas security official in Gaza
articles.summary: Abu Nahl, 50, was killed in a crowded area leaving four others, including a Palestinian woman, wounded.
articles.body:
An Israeli strike on Gaza has killed a senior Hamas security official and wounded several others, according to local authorities.

The deceased senior Hamas official has been identified as Brigadier General Naim Abu Nahl, who was the director of Hamas’s internal security apparatus in Gaza, medics and police said on Tuesday. Gaza’s Ministry of Interior and National Security confirmed the death.

Abu Nahl was 50 years old and Director General of the Internal Security Office across the Gaza Strip. A statement from Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the security official was walking in the street when a drone strike killed him.

Four others, including a Palestinian woman, were wounded and taken to al-Shifa Medical Complex. The area where the missile struck is crowded with displaced people and shelters.

Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the assassination came after the Internal Security Service had made significant gains against what it described as “gangs collaborating with the occupation and operating in areas under Israeli military control.”

The Israeli army and the Shin Bet domestic security service said in a joint statement they had struck a senior Hamas figure, without identifying him, adding that further details would be provided later. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan later said the target was Abu Nahl. Citing Israeli sources, Kan said Abu Nahl had succeeded Moein al-Arbeid, who was detained by the Israeli army and Shin Bet during a special operation in September and remains in Israeli custody.

Several Palestinians were already reported killed earlier on Tuesday , including a child and police officers, while dozens were injured in Israeli air strikes on various parts of the Gaza Strip, according to local health officials.

There have been daily violations of the so-called “ceasefire” in Gaza, with Israeli air strikes continuing regularly in its genocidal war, with at least 1,680 people killed and 6,100 injured since the ceasefire was signed on October 11 last year.

articles.title: Could Russia-Ukraine war threaten Libya’s fragile reunification process?
articles.summary: Ukraine’s involvement in Libya raises concerns as Zelenskyy admits targeting Russian vessels in a key port city.
articles.body:
The recent attack on a Russian warship in the port of Benghazi, Libya, has drawn condemnation from both sides of the country’s fractured political landscape.

On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took responsibility for the drone strikes on the Russian ship docked in the Libyan port a day earlier.

This led to outcry from Libyan officials from both sides of the political divide, who fear the attack threatens fragile efforts to unify the country after more than a decade of war and division.

What is behind the Russian presence in Libya?

Since the fall of longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, Libya’s fractious political landscape has settled into two rival administrations currently governing the country: the internationally recognised Government of National Unity (GNU) based in the western city of Tripoli and led by interim Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and authorities linked to renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar in the eastern city of Benghazi.

Haftar, who had moved to the United States when Gaddafi was still the leader, has long cultivated close ties with Russia. Moscow has allegedly provided his self-described Libyan National Army (LNA) with weapons, mercenaries and diplomatic backing, key to helping him consolidate control over much of the east.

In exchange, Russia has retained a military and logistical foothold in the country, including ports, airfields, storage, maintenance capacity, and overland routes critical to supporting its operations in the rest of Africa.

Russia is believed to have a military presence in Sudan, Mali, the Central African Republic, Niger, Burkina Faso, among others.

There are an estimated 1,000 to 1,800 Russian personnel in Libya, including from its Africa Corps, a unit within Moscow’s Ministry of Defence, which has tried to bring Russian private military companies in Africa under government control.

The importance of eastern Libya as a military hub for Russia only increased after Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, a key regional ally of Moscow, fell from power in December 2024, said Ruslan Trad, nonresident fellow of Global Security at the Atlantic Council.

“Russia’s bases in Libya are less about fighting in Libya itself than about sustaining Moscow’s wider military and political footprint across the Sahel and Central Africa. They function as a logistics bridge between the Mediterranean and Russia’s partners and deployments deeper in the continent,” Trad told Al Jazeera.

“Without this hub, Russia would have to sustain operations thousands of kilometres from Russia with far fewer reliable transit options.”

Why is there a Ukrainian presence in Libya?

The internationally recognised government in Tripoli has sought to counterbalance Russia’s involvement in Libya by forming its own international partnerships, most notably with Turkiye. The GNU has also adopted a firmly pro-Ukraine stance in recent years.

In 2022, the GNU issued an unqualified condemnation of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. It was the only Arab country to vote in favour of suspending Russia’s participation in the United Nations Human Rights Council later that year.

The relationship between the GNU and Ukraine deepened in 2023, with Prime Minister Dbeibah pushing for the establishment of an official embassy in Tripoli and opening talks on military cooperation. Shortly thereafter, Ukrainian forces began providing training and technical support to GNU forces.

Russia has long accused Ukraine of arming GNU forces and maintaining a presence in western Libya to target its interests in Africa, including a string of unclaimed attacks on Russian-linked vessels off Libya’s coast in recent months suspected to have been carried out by Ukrainian forces. Zelenskyy’s claim of responsibility for Sunday’s attack left no room for ambiguity.

“Ukraine’s presence in northwestern Libya is a limited, discreet military cooperation arrangement with the Government of National Unity,” Trad said. “Its main function is to support long-range drone operations against Russian shipping and military logistics in the Mediterranean.”

Suspected Ukrainian attacks in the Mediterranean include drone attacks in September on the Russian cargo ship, Lady Mariia, between Crete and Libya, and an attack that set Russian LNG carrier Arctic Metagaz ablaze in December, leaving it adrift between Malta and Libya.

But it is not clear whether Sunday’s attack was launched from Libyan soil.

Groups loyal to the GNU and Haftar’s LNA have fought a gruelling war since 2014, with thousands killed. Efforts to reconcile the eastern and western authorities have repeatedly failed.

Since 2025, regional and international efforts to bridge Libya’s divide have yielded cautious progress, resulting in a cooperation framework that seeks to unify the country’s political, military and economic institutions.

In April, Libya adopted a unified national budget for the first time in more than a decade. The move was welcomed in a joint statement by 10 countries involved in Libya’s conflict or the process to end it, including the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, France, Germany, Italy, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, the United Kingdom and the US.

Russia also welcomed the move in an April 22 statement but warned against the involvement of “external actors” in shaping Libya’s future.

On August 30, the two sides agreed to presidential and legislative elections within 24 months under a single executive authority, in a UN-mediated deal, but questions still linger over their commitments to the process.

Sansom Milton, a senior research fellow at the Doha-based Center for Conflict and Humanitarian Studies, told Al Jazeera that the framework remained the clearest opening for a political settlement between the two rivals in years.

“The Haftar and Dbeibah camps have moved from bargaining over how to share Libya’s oil wealth to how they might share power,” Milton said. “I doubt Sunday’s strikes alone will derail talks.”

Osama Kubbar, a Libyan political and security analyst, agreed that the attack as an independent action by the Ukrainian government was unlikely to disrupt the political process.

“If the boats did indeed depart from Tripoli, it was an independent action by Ukrainian personnel who are primarily present to train Libyan forces in the west of the country,” he said. “It will therefore not affect the reconciliation process between the two sides.”

The condemnation of the attack by both sides could be counterproductive to any Ukrainian efforts to establish a presence in Libya, analysts told Al Jazeera.

“Both the Russian state and the Haftar family will feel compelled to retaliate – somehow. I’m not saying it’s going to be easy, but the pressure is going to be there, because what happened was humiliating for both,” Harchaoui told Al Jazeera.

“So now that this actor, Ukraine, is not just performing covert action, but overt actions against components of the Russian state, then it opens up all sorts of possibilities.”

It could also have an impact on the fragile peace process in Libya, with the country ever sensitive to a new round of conflict.

“I’m not saying it’s likely, but the possibility now can be imagined,” Harchaoui said.

Both administrations insist that they do not want a foreign war between Russia and Ukraine brought to Libya’s shores.

Mousa al-Koni, one of the three members of the Presidential Council that acts as head of state for the country under a UN deal, characterised the attack as “terrorist” and promised legal and diplomatic measures against culprits, including referring the incident to the UN Security Council.

Ukraine will also face further pressure from both sides to limit its role in Libya.

“Both sides have an interest in framing the strike as a violation of Libyan sovereignty,” Trad said. “What follows will likely be less a clean expulsion than a reduction in visibility and control.”
