articles.title: 2 years, 500 trips: 4,474t plastic waste moved from Trichy to Ariyalur cement plant
articles.summary: Trichy Corporation sent 4,474 tonnes of non-recyclable plastic in 500 trips over 2 years to an Ariyalur cement plant for RDF kiln fuel, reducing landfill.
articles.body: Trichy: Trichy corporation has completed 500 trips in sending non-recyclable and non-resaleable plastic waste to a private cement factory in Ariyalur district where it is utilized as refuse derived fuel (RDF) to power kilns. In the last two years, more than 4,474 tonnes of plastic waste has been scientifically disposed of by the local body, which otherwise would have ended up as landfill in the city’s Ariyamangalam dump yard.Trichy city on average generates 450-460 tonnes of municipal solid waste a day. About 52% of the waste is biodegradable (kitchen and food waste), and 32% is non-biodegradable, such as recyclable plastics, clothes, metal, and rubber materials. About 16% of the waste accounts as neither recyclable nor saleable (inert waste) materials. While the local body segregates and makes manure from the biodegradable waste at 38 micro compost centres, non-biodegradable waste such as metal and glass items are sold to scrap dealers.However, single-use and multi-layer plastic heads to Ariyamangalam dump yard as landfill. In Sept 2024, the local body entered into an MoU with Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Limited, Ariyalur, to supply 300 tonnes of inert waste a month to be used as RFD to power kilns. As of Nov 24, 2026, Trichy corporation has completed 500 trips in sending RDF to the cement plant. The local body’s own truck is utilized to transport the waste to the Ariyalur factory.The plastic waste sent from the city is shredded and loaded into kilns in the cement factory to manufacture clinkers. “Five collection points, one each in five zones, have sent 600-1,000 tonnes of plastic waste each. We are in the process of expanding the practice to rope in more cement plants. Additional vehicles through CSR drive are considered,” Kishore Mohan, operations head, SR Vedhaah, the local body’s outsourcing partner, said.Officials said that if the 4,474 tonnes was dumped at Ariyamangalam instead of being sent to the cement plant, only the biomining process could scientifically reclaim them but at very high cost. Trichy corporation is also providing manure to residents at one rupee a kg through 38 MCCs. articles.title: Former NFL star Mike Alstott's foundation spent Thanksgiving week delivering holiday meals to Florida firefighters working away from their families, including crews across 48 Hillsborough County fire stations
articles.summary: As the holiday season approaches, many people will be working around the clock to keep their communities safe.
articles.body: As the holiday season approaches, many people will be working around the clock to keep their communities safe. Firefighters are among those spending the holidays on duty, often putting in 24-hour shifts away from their families. Former Tampa Bay Buccaneers star Mike Alstott is making sure these first responders don't miss out on a traditional Thanksgiving meal, with his family foundation stepping in to serve firefighters at all 48 Hillsborough County fire stations and the emergency dispatch centre. It was the eighth consecutive year the foundation had distributed holiday meals.A care package for the first respondersAs Thanksgiving approaches, the Mike Alstott Family Foundation has begun distributing holiday meals to firefighters. The foundation is serving 48 different fire stations in Hillsborough County, as well as several in Pinellas County, for the holidays, according to a report by News 34. Each holiday meal package included turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, vegetables, gravy, cheesecake and ground coffee, according to the foundation's announcement. The idea is simple. Crews who are on shift can prepare a holiday meal at the station instead of eating something quick. Firefighters and dispatchers who work on Thanksgiving spend the day away from their families. Many stations celebrate together, and the foundation said the donation is meant to make that shared table feel more special.Alstott delivered the meals in personAlstott, a former Tampa Bay Buccaneers fullback and a member of the team's Ring of Honour, was at headquarters to hand out the groceries. He described the gesture as a way to thank the first responders, who work around the clock to keep the community safe. “These firefighter men and women that are on duty at that time, on Thanksgiving, they’re away from their families, and the least that we can do is provide them with a turkey meal and be able to say thank you,” Mike Alstott said.He said he was grateful for the support of his family and the foundation's sponsors. "I'm blessed to be able to provide and have all these great people behind me, my family, and the foundation," Alstott said. He also said the handshakes mattered most. "When you're able to shake the hands of each individual and stuff like that and say thank you, that's where it really counts in the heart," he added.Alstott said several sponsors, including Warner Logistics, Tito's, Bill Currie Ford, Jeoffrey's Coffee and Bassano's, had joined the initiative. Interestingly, this was the eighth consecutive year the foundation had supplied Hillsborough County stations, according to the county's fire rescue department.Alstott started the foundation in 2007, hoping to give back to his community. "It's an honor to give back to our first responders and specifically Hillsborough County Fire Rescue for this Thanksgiving holiday," Alstott, who delivered the meals in person with his team added.Meanwhile, Hillsborough County Fire Chief Rob Herrin said the donation means a lot to crews who rarely receive public gestures of thanks."We're on duty 24/7, so we eat at the fire station, so we are away from our families for Thanksgiving," Herrin said. "For the Alstott Foundation to provide an entire Thanksgiving meal for our firefighters is tremendous."The chief also said that firefighters give a great deal to the community without receiving much in return. These gifts therefore mean a lot to the first responders. "They give so much, and for them to be given to by the Mike Alstott Foundation is something we are not used to. To be honest with you, it really puts a smile on a lot of faces,” he said.Thanksgiving falls on Thursday, 26 November, this year. articles.title: Iran’s leaders want a baby boom. A struggling economy stands in the way
articles.summary: Iran risks growing old before it becomes prosperous, with decades of crippling US sanctions and economic mismanagement leaving it ill-equipped to absorb the financial burden.
articles.body: Iran must address its declining population by encouraging young people to marry and have children, according to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The country of 93 million faces a demographic crisis, with an aging population and falling birthrate as young couples struggle to afford homes and start families amid a deepening economic slump. In a statement attributed to him on Tuesday, Khamenei said Iran must address shortcomings in past population policies, describing population growth as a “strategic priority.” His message was read at a ceremony for the National Population Rejuvenation Award, which honors efforts to help families and increase Iran’s birth rate. Khamenei, who has not made a public appearance since becoming Supreme Leader in March, urged officials to make it easier for young people to marry, support childbearing, improve individual health and promote “a family-centered culture” to help Iran overcome what he called “a critical period.” His message follows several warnings from Iranian officials about the consequences of a spiraling rate of marriages and births. “The country’s demographic situation is extremely critical,” Marzieh Vahid Dastjerdi, secretary of the National Population Headquarters, said last month. The fertility rate has fallen from 6.7 children per woman in the 1980s to 1.34, Dastjerdi said, with several provinces now seeing their populations decline as a result. “If we do not act today to reverse the decline in marriage and childbearing, our demographic opportunities will be lost one after another,” she said, predicting that the country’s population could shrink by two-thirds to just 31 million over the next 75 years. The speed at which Iran’s population is aging makes it a demographic outlier in the Middle East, where many countries are grappling with challenges of growing youth populations. In less than two decades, Iran has transitioned from a youthful and fast-growing society into below-replacement fertility. Unlike advanced economies facing similar demographic challenges, Iran risks growing old before it becomes prosperous, with decades of crippling US sanctions and economic mismanagement leaving it ill-equipped to absorb the financial burden of an aging population. One Iranian official called the country’s demographic trend a “mega-crisis.” The number of births registered in 2012 was 1.3 million. In 2025, it was 892,000. Over the same period, the percentage of the population aged 14 and younger declined from 25.3% to 15.8%. At the other end of the scale, the population aged 60 and over rose from 8.2% to 12.6%. Decline in marriage Unless the trend is reversed, the over-sixties will account for nearly a third of the population by 2050. And caring for that aging segment of society will become more arduous. “The growing trend of one-child families in recent years has created numerous educational, psychological and social problems,” according to Fatemeh Mohammadbeigi, who serves on the parliament’s health commission. Within about 15 years, each young couple may have to care for two sets of elderly parents without any siblings to share the responsibility, she said. At the heart of the crisis is a sharp decline in marriage. The number of marriages fell by more than 50% between 2011 and this year, according to figures from Iran’s Civil Registration Organization. It attributed the fall to economic pressures such as inflation, rising housing costs, unemployment, and the growing difficulty of affording the expenses of starting a family. Eighteen million Iranians of marriageable age are still single, including 10 million men and 8 million women, according to state media. Roughly 2.4 million women over 35 are single. “All of our population-related issues are tied to marriage,” Dastjerdi said last month. But the country’s demographic problems are also partly the result of its own policies. The Islamic Republic introduced a major family planning program in the late 1980s – offering free contraceptives and vasectomies and later scrapping some benefits for larger families – only to reverse course decades later. Iran’s rapidly changing demography has played out starkly in the capital, Tehran, this year, amid the perpetual economic crunch. Births have fallen nearly 10%, and deaths have risen more than 6% since March, compared to last year. Women are selling their hair Iran is one of the world’s biggest producers of oil and gas, but its economy is likely to shrink by 7.6% this year, according to the International Monetary Fund, thanks to the US naval blockade that has brought seaborne foreign trade to a near halt, damage to infrastructure since the conflict began in February, and ongoing sanctions. A lack of employment opportunities and growing poverty discourage young people from getting married. Iranians increasingly use credit apps to get by, incurring more debt. Online advertisements have begun appearing, offering basic food products for sale in installments. One can of tuna, priced at the equivalent of just over $1, was being offered in four installments. Some young women have taken desperate steps to make ends meet – including selling their hair to be made into extensions. Among those seeking to sell their hair are female heads of household, mothers trying to cover the cost of their children’s medical treatment and students struggling to pay for their education, according to a recent study. “At first, I wanted to sell my laptop, but I needed it to write my thesis. So I decided to sell my hair instead. Hair grows back, but I can’t get back the time I would lose on my thesis,” Maryam, a 27-year-old master’s student, told the Iranian outlet Fararu. Millions of young Iranians are focused on getting by rather than planning for the future. Earlier this month, the official media outlet ILNA, which has been outspoken in reporting hardships among Iranians, said that poverty was at “unprecedented levels, leaving unemployed people, seasonal workers, single mothers, low-wage earners, and even skilled workers, nurses and teachers struggling to afford basic necessities.” It also pointed to rising school dropout rates, giving some of tomorrow’s prospective parents even less chance of affording a family.
